Main_Paragraph: Known as the Island of the Gods, Bali is Indonesia's most visited island, where volcanic peaks, emerald rice terraces and centuries-old Hindu temples sit alongside palm-fringed beaches. Our Bali holidays take you beyond the resorts of the south coast into the island's cultural heart in Ubud, through terraced rice fields protected by a UNESCO-listed irrigation system, and into ancient temple complexes where daily offerings and colourful ceremonies are still very much part of everyday life.
Subtitle: About our Bali holidays
Paragraph1: Ubud is Bali's spiritual and cultural centre, a world away from the beach clubs of Seminyak and Kuta. Surrounded by jungle and rice paddies, the town is known for traditional dance performances, art markets and yoga studios, and makes an ideal base for exploring the temples and terraced hillsides of central Bali.
Paragraph2: The Tegallalang and Jatiluwih rice terraces cascade down the volcanic slopes around Ubud in perfectly sculpted emerald steps. They're maintained by subak, a centuries-old cooperative irrigation system dating back to the 9th century, which has earned UNESCO World Heritage status for the way it reflects the Balinese philosophy of harmony between people, nature and the spiritual world.
Paragraph3: Ornate temple gates and shrines appear on almost every street in Bali, and our tours introduce you to some of the island's most significant sites - from the clifftop sea temple of Uluwatu to Pura Samuan Tiga in Gianyar, a 10th-century temple whose name means 'meeting of the three', built to mark the unification of Bali's Hindu sects under the Warmadewa dynasty.
Paragraph4: The Bukit Peninsula in the south is home to some of Bali's most dramatic coastline, with Uluwatu Temple perched on cliffs high above the Indian Ocean. It's one of the island's most visited sites, especially at sunset, when traditional Kecak fire dance performances are held against the backdrop of the sea.

Main_Paragraph: Bali has a tropical climate with fairly stable temperatures of around 26-32°C throughout the year, so there's rarely a bad time to visit. The dry season runs from April to September and is generally considered the best time to go, with sunny days that suit temple visits, diving and trekking; August is usually the driest month. The wet season runs from October to March, bringing short, heavy tropical downpours - usually in the afternoon - alongside lush, green landscapes and quieter temples. If you'd like good weather without the peak-season crowds of July and August, May, June and September are usually the sweet spot.
when_to_go: When to go to Bali, month by month
when_to_go_html: May, June and September usually offer the best balance of dry weather and lighter crowds. July and August are the driest months but also the busiest and most expensive, coinciding with European summer holidays. The wet season (October to March) brings short afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain, and January is typically the wettest month. Balinese Hindu ceremonies and temple festivals take place year-round on the 210-day pawukon calendar, so it's worth checking local dates before you travel.
